title: Chemistry Practical I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L quantitative analytical chemistry laboratory curriculum, paired with the CHM207/CHM208 lecture courses: acid-base, redox, complexometric and precipitation titrations, gravimetric analysis, basic colorimetric/spectrophotometric determination, standard solution preparation, and volumetric calculations/data treatment.

questions.question: Before any titration is performed in a quantitative analysis practical, the burette must first be:
options: Rinsed with distilled water only and used while still wet with water
Rinsed two or three times with small portions of the titrant solution to be used
Filled directly from the reagent bottle without any rinsing
Dried in an oven at 150 degC before filling
questions.correct_answer: Rinsed two or three times with small portions of the titrant solution to be used
questions.explanation: Rinsing the burette with the titrant itself removes residual water that would otherwise dilute the titrant and introduce a systematic error into the recorded titre.

questions.question: A student titrates 25.0 cm3 of a sodium hydroxide solution against 0.100 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid, using phenolphthalein indicator, and requires 22.50 cm3 of acid to reach the endpoint. What is the concentration of the NaOH solution?
options: 0.100 mol/dm3
0.111 mol/dm3
0.225 mol/dm3
questions.explanation: NaOH + HCl react 1:1. Moles HCl = 0.02250 dm3 x 0.100 mol/dm3 = 0.00225 mol = moles NaOH. Concentration NaOH = 0.00225 mol / 0.0250 dm3 = 0.0900 mol/dm3.

questions.question: In a titration practical, why should the conical flask be swirled continuously while titrant is added from the burette?
options: To ensure thorough, rapid mixing so the indicator responds accurately to the true endpoint and localized excess titrant is avoided
To cool the solution during the reaction
To evaporate excess solvent from the flask
Swirling has no real purpose and can be skipped
questions.correct_answer: To ensure thorough, rapid mixing so the indicator responds accurately to the true endpoint and localized excess titrant is avoided
questions.explanation: Continuous swirling ensures the titrant is evenly mixed as it is added, preventing localized over-titration and allowing the colour change at the true endpoint to be observed sharply and reliably.

questions.question: A titration is generally repeated until at least two 'concordant' titre values are obtained. Concordant titres are those that:
options: Agree with each other within about 0.1 cm3
Differ from each other by more than 5 cm3
Are obtained using different indicators each time
Are always exactly equal to the first titration performed
questions.correct_answer: Agree with each other within about 0.1 cm3
questions.explanation: Concordant results (typically within 0.1 cm3 of each other) indicate that random error has been minimized and that the average of these titres can be reliably used in the subsequent calculation.

questions.question: In a redox titration in which potassium permanganate is used as the titrant to determine iron(II) in an acidified solution, dilute sulphuric acid rather than hydrochloric acid is used to acidify the sample because:
options: Chloride ions can be oxidized by permanganate, introducing a side reaction that gives an inaccurate (too high) titre
Hydrochloric acid is more expensive than sulphuric acid
Sulphuric acid changes the colour of permanganate
Hydrochloric acid reacts with iron(II) to form a precipitate
questions.correct_answer: Chloride ions can be oxidized by permanganate, introducing a side reaction that gives an inaccurate (too high) titre
questions.explanation: Permanganate can oxidize chloride ion (especially catalytically in the presence of Fe2+/Fe3+), consuming extra titrant in a side reaction and giving a falsely high result, so sulphuric acid (whose sulphate ion is not readily oxidized) is used instead.

questions.question: In the permanganate titration of iron(II), the endpoint is signalled by:
options: The appearance of a faint permanent pink colour, as KMnO4 is self-indicating and the solution was colourless/pale beforehand
The solution suddenly turning bright yellow
Formation of a white precipitate
A sudden drop in temperature of the solution
questions.correct_answer: The appearance of a faint permanent pink colour, as KMnO4 is self-indicating and the solution was colourless/pale beforehand
questions.explanation: As permanganate reacts with Fe2+ it is reduced to the nearly colourless Mn2+; once all Fe2+ is consumed, the next drop of KMnO4 remains unreacted, imparting a persistent faint pink colour that marks the endpoint.

questions.question: In an iodometric titration to determine an oxidizing agent such as copper(II), excess potassium iodide is first added to generate iodine, which is then titrated against standard sodium thiosulfate solution. Starch indicator should be added:
options: Near the endpoint, once the iodine colour has faded to a pale straw/yellow, rather than at the very start of the titration
At the very beginning of the titration, before any thiosulfate is added
Only after the titration is already complete
Directly to the solid potassium iodide before dissolving it
questions.correct_answer: Near the endpoint, once the iodine colour has faded to a pale straw/yellow, rather than at the very start of the titration
questions.explanation: Adding starch too early, while iodine concentration is still high, can cause the starch-iodine complex to form irreversibly and give a less sharp endpoint, so starch is conventionally added only once the solution has faded to pale yellow, close to the endpoint.

questions.question: In an EDTA complexometric titration used to determine total water hardness, Eriochrome Black T indicator is added and the solution is buffered to about pH 10 using an ammonia buffer. Why is this specific pH range needed?
options: Eriochrome Black T only gives a clear, sharp colour change with the metal ions in this pH range, and EDTA's complexing ability with Ca2+/Mg2+ is also favourable there
The pH has no effect on the titration and any pH would work equally well
At pH 10 the metal ions precipitate completely as hydroxides before titration begins
Ammonia buffer is used only to add a pleasant odour to the solution
questions.correct_answer: Eriochrome Black T only gives a clear, sharp colour change with the metal ions in this pH range, and EDTA's complexing ability with Ca2+/Mg2+ is also favourable there
questions.explanation: Eriochrome Black T's colour transition and the stability of the EDTA-metal complexes are both pH-dependent, and the ammonia buffer at about pH 10 provides the range where the indicator changes sharply from wine-red to blue at the equivalence point.

questions.question: In Mohr's method for determining chloride ion by titration with standard silver nitrate solution, using potassium chromate as indicator, the titration must be carried out at approximately neutral pH because:
options: In strongly acidic solution the chromate indicator is converted to dichromate and will not form the coloured silver chromate precipitate properly, while in strongly basic solution silver hydroxide may precipitate
Chloride ions dissolve completely in acidic solution and cannot be titrated
Silver nitrate only dissolves in neutral solution
The reaction requires ultraviolet light to proceed at any other pH
questions.correct_answer: In strongly acidic solution the chromate indicator is converted to dichromate and will not form the coloured silver chromate precipitate properly, while in strongly basic solution silver hydroxide may precipitate
questions.explanation: Mohr's method requires a near-neutral pH (about 6.5-9) because chromate is protonated to dichromate under acidic conditions (impairing the indicator response) while silver hydroxide or silver oxide can form under strongly basic conditions.

questions.question: In gravimetric analysis, after a precipitate has been filtered, it is typically washed with a dilute solution of a suitable electrolyte rather than pure distilled water, mainly to:
options: Prevent peptization (redispersion into a colloid) of the precipitate while still removing soluble impurities
Increase the total mass of the final precipitate
Dissolve the precipitate completely for easier filtration
Change the precipitate into a different, more soluble compound
questions.correct_answer: Prevent peptization (redispersion into a colloid) of the precipitate while still removing soluble impurities
questions.explanation: Washing with pure water can strip away the adsorbed electrolyte layer that keeps a freshly formed precipitate coagulated, causing it to disperse (peptize) and pass through the filter, so a dilute volatile electrolyte solution is used instead.

questions.question: In gravimetric analysis, a filtered precipitate is dried or ignited and weighed repeatedly until 'constant weight' is achieved. This means:
options: Successive weighings after further heating agree closely, confirming that moisture and volatile matter have been fully removed
The crucible has reached its melting point
The mass has become exactly zero
The precipitate has changed colour permanently
questions.correct_answer: Successive weighings after further heating agree closely, confirming that moisture and volatile matter have been fully removed
questions.explanation: Constant weight is confirmed when repeated cycles of heating, cooling in a desiccator, and weighing give essentially unchanged mass readings, showing all volatile material has been driven off.

questions.question: Before weighing a hot crucible and precipitate on an analytical balance, the crucible should first be:
options: Cooled in a desiccator to room temperature, to avoid convection currents affecting the balance reading and to prevent moisture reabsorption
Weighed immediately while still hot, for the fastest possible result
Placed directly in water to cool it rapidly
Left uncovered on the open bench to cool
questions.correct_answer: Cooled in a desiccator to room temperature, to avoid convection currents affecting the balance reading and to prevent moisture reabsorption
questions.explanation: A hot object creates air convection currents that give inaccurate balance readings, and cooling in a desiccator (rather than in the open) also prevents the sample from reabsorbing atmospheric moisture before weighing.

questions.question: To prepare 250.0 cm3 of a standard solution from a precisely weighed solid, the correct procedure after dissolving the solid in a small volume of solvent in a beaker is to:
options: Quantitatively transfer the solution into a 250 cm3 volumetric flask, rinse the beaker into the flask, and make up to the calibration mark with solvent
Discard the beaker solution and start again directly in the flask
Pour the solution into any convenient container and estimate the volume by eye
Leave the solution in the original beaker indefinitely
questions.correct_answer: Quantitatively transfer the solution into a 250 cm3 volumetric flask, rinse the beaker into the flask, and make up to the calibration mark with solvent
questions.explanation: Quantitative transfer, including rinsing the beaker and stirring rod into the flask, ensures no solute is lost, and making up to the calibration mark at the correct temperature gives a solution of accurately known concentration.

questions.question: A student needs to prepare 500 cm3 of a 0.0500 mol/dm3 standard solution of anhydrous sodium carbonate (Na2CO3, molar mass 106 g/mol). What mass of Na2CO3 must be weighed out?
questions.explanation: Moles required = 0.0500 mol/dm3 x 0.500 dm3 = 0.0250 mol. Mass = 0.0250 mol x 106 g/mol = 2.65 g.

questions.question: Why is solid sodium hydroxide unsuitable for preparing a standard solution of accurately known concentration directly by weighing?
options: It is hygroscopic and readily absorbs both moisture and carbon dioxide from the air, so its true purity at the point of weighing is not exactly known
Sodium hydroxide cannot dissolve in water at all
Sodium hydroxide reacts violently and explosively with air
It has an unusually low, imprecisely known molar mass
questions.correct_answer: It is hygroscopic and readily absorbs both moisture and carbon dioxide from the air, so its true purity at the point of weighing is not exactly known
questions.explanation: Because solid NaOH absorbs atmospheric water and CO2, a freshly weighed sample is never exactly pure NaOH, so its solution must instead be standardized against a primary standard such as potassium hydrogen phthalate.

questions.question: A student is instructed to standardize a hydrochloric acid solution using anhydrous sodium carbonate as the primary standard, with methyl orange as indicator. Near the endpoint, the solution is typically boiled briefly and then re-titrated to a final colour change. This boiling step is done to:
options: Expel dissolved carbon dioxide formed during the reaction, since its presence can cause a premature or indistinct colour change
Increase the concentration of the hydrochloric acid
Destroy the methyl orange indicator
Speed up evaporation of all the water in the flask
questions.correct_answer: Expel dissolved carbon dioxide formed during the reaction, since its presence can cause a premature or indistinct colour change
questions.explanation: As carbonate reacts with acid, dissolved CO2 (carbonic acid) forms and can cause the indicator to change colour prematurely; brief boiling drives off this CO2, sharpening the true endpoint upon cooling and further titration.

questions.question: In a colorimetric practical determination of the concentration of an unknown coloured solution, a series of standard solutions of known concentration is prepared mainly in order to:
options: Construct a calibration curve of absorbance against concentration, from which the concentration of the unknown can be interpolated
Provide extra solution in case the unknown sample is spilled
Change the colour of the unknown solution
Calibrate the balance used to weigh solid reagents
questions.correct_answer: Construct a calibration curve of absorbance against concentration, from which the concentration of the unknown can be interpolated
questions.explanation: Measuring the absorbance of several accurately known standard concentrations allows a calibration (Beer's law) plot to be constructed, against which the absorbance of an unknown sample can be compared to determine its concentration.

questions.question: In a colorimetric practical, the instrument is 'zeroed' or 'blanked' using a cell containing the solvent and reagents but no analyte. If this blanking step is omitted, the resulting absorbance readings for all subsequent samples will be:
options: Systematically shifted, since absorbance from the solvent/reagents/cell is included in each reading and not accounted for
Completely unaffected by the omission
Automatically corrected by the instrument regardless of the operator's actions
Always exactly zero
questions.correct_answer: Systematically shifted, since absorbance from the solvent/reagents/cell is included in each reading and not accounted for
questions.explanation: Failing to blank the instrument means the recorded absorbance includes a constant background contribution from the solvent, reagents, and cuvette, introducing a systematic error into every measurement made afterward.

questions.question: When handling a glass cuvette for spectrophotometric measurement, the operator should avoid touching the clear optical faces of the cell mainly because:
options: Fingerprints and smudges can scatter or absorb light, introducing error into the absorbance reading
Touching the cell changes the molar absorptivity of the analyte
The cell will shatter immediately if touched
Fingerprints increase the effective path length of the cell
questions.correct_answer: Fingerprints and smudges can scatter or absorb light, introducing error into the absorbance reading
questions.explanation: Smudges or fingerprints on the optical faces of a cuvette can scatter or absorb light independently of the sample, giving a falsely elevated or inconsistent absorbance reading, so cells are handled by their ribbed/frosted sides.

questions.question: In quantitative analysis practical reports, a 'blank titration' is performed by titrating all reagents except the actual analyte. Its titre value is then:
options: Subtracted from the sample titre, to correct for titrant consumed by the reagents/indicator alone rather than by the analyte
Added directly to the sample titre without correction
Ignored completely and never reported
Used in place of the sample titration altogether
questions.correct_answer: Subtracted from the sample titre, to correct for titrant consumed by the reagents/indicator alone rather than by the analyte
questions.explanation: A blank titration measures any titrant consumed by side reactions (e.g., with the indicator or reagent impurities) in the absence of analyte, and this volume is subtracted from the sample titre so the calculation reflects only the analyte's reaction.

questions.question: In a practical determination of the percentage purity of an impure sample of a solid acid by titration, the general calculation approach is to:
options: Use the titre volume and known concentration of the standard base to find moles of acid reacted, convert to mass of pure acid, then express this as a percentage of the total sample mass weighed out
Simply weigh the sample before and after titration and calculate the mass lost
Assume the sample is 100% pure and skip any calculation
Compare the colour intensity of the sample to a reference chart only
questions.correct_answer: Use the titre volume and known concentration of the standard base to find moles of acid reacted, convert to mass of pure acid, then express this as a percentage of the total sample mass weighed out
questions.explanation: Percentage purity by titration is found by using titration stoichiometry to calculate the mass of pure active acid actually present, then dividing this by the total mass of impure sample weighed and multiplying by 100.

questions.question: In recording data for a titration practical, the initial and final burette readings should each be recorded to the nearest:
options: 0.05 cm3, reflecting the smallest graduation the burette can reliably be read to, including one estimated digit
Whole 10 cm3
Whole litre
Nearest 1 cm3 only, since more precision is unnecessary
questions.correct_answer: 0.05 cm3, reflecting the smallest graduation the burette can reliably be read to, including one estimated digit
questions.explanation: A standard burette is graduated in 0.1 cm3 divisions, and good practice is to estimate and record readings to the nearest 0.05 cm3, reflecting the true precision of the instrument.

questions.question: A student obtains three titre values of 24.50, 24.55, and 28.10 cm3 in a titration practical. The correct treatment of this data set is to:
options: Discard the clearly outlying 28.10 cm3 value and average only the two concordant results, 24.50 and 24.55 cm3
Average all three values including the outlier without question
Discard all three values and report no result
Use only the largest value, 28.10 cm3, as the final answer
questions.correct_answer: Discard the clearly outlying 28.10 cm3 value and average only the two concordant results, 24.50 and 24.55 cm3
questions.explanation: A titre that differs substantially from concordant replicate values (here 28.10 cm3, likely due to a procedural error) is reasonably excluded, and the mean of the genuinely concordant results (24.50 and 24.55 cm3) is used for the calculation.

questions.question: In a practical determination of water hardness by EDTA titration, the result is often expressed as an equivalent concentration of calcium carbonate (mg/dm3 as CaCO3) because:
options: It provides a standard, conventional way to express total hardness due to both calcium and magnesium ions on a single common scale
Calcium carbonate is the only ion that causes hardness
CaCO3 is the titrant used in the reaction
Magnesium ions cannot be measured by EDTA titration at all
questions.correct_answer: It provides a standard, conventional way to express total hardness due to both calcium and magnesium ions on a single common scale
questions.explanation: Total hardness is conventionally reported in units equivalent to mg/dm3 of CaCO3, providing a standardized way to compare hardness values even though both Ca2+ and Mg2+ (and other divalent ions) contribute to the overall EDTA titre.

questions.question: A student weighs an empty crucible, then weighs it again after adding a precipitate and drying it. To find the mass of the precipitate alone, the student should:
options: Subtract the mass of the empty crucible from the mass of the crucible plus dried precipitate
Add the two masses together
Use only the mass of the empty crucible
Divide the two masses by each other
questions.correct_answer: Subtract the mass of the empty crucible from the mass of the crucible plus dried precipitate
questions.explanation: The mass of the precipitate itself is obtained by taking the difference between the mass of the crucible with the dried precipitate and the mass of the empty (tared) crucible.

questions.question: During filtration of a precipitate using filter paper and a funnel, the filter paper is folded and fitted into the funnel, and a small amount of solvent is used to seal it against the funnel wall. This is done mainly to:
options: Ensure a good seal so that liquid passes only through the paper, not around its edges, giving efficient and complete filtration
Dissolve the precipitate for easier collection
Increase the rate of crystallization of the precipitate
Prevent any liquid from passing through the filter paper at all
questions.correct_answer: Ensure a good seal so that liquid passes only through the paper, not around its edges, giving efficient and complete filtration
questions.explanation: Wetting and seating the filter paper snugly against the funnel forms a seal that prevents liquid from bypassing the paper around its edges, ensuring that all suspended precipitate is properly retained on the filter.

questions.question: In the standardization of a potassium permanganate solution using standard ammonium iron(II) sulfate (Mohr's salt) as the reducing primary standard, why is potassium permanganate not used as a primary standard directly?
options: Solid KMnO4 is never sufficiently pure and stable, and its solutions slowly decompose (partly catalyzed by light and by MnO2), so its exact concentration must be established by titration against a suitable primary standard
Permanganate reacts explosively with water and cannot be dissolved
Permanganate solutions have no measurable colour
Iron(II) sulfate cannot react with permanganate at all
questions.correct_answer: Solid KMnO4 is never sufficiently pure and stable, and its solutions slowly decompose (partly catalyzed by light and by MnO2), so its exact concentration must be established by titration against a suitable primary standard
questions.explanation: Because permanganate solutions gradually decompose and are difficult to obtain in perfectly pure, stable solid form, they are treated as secondary standards and their exact concentration is determined by standardizing against a primary standard such as Mohr's salt or oxalic acid.

questions.question: A pipette filler (rubber bulb or mechanical pipette pump) is used instead of mouth pipetting in a modern analytical chemistry laboratory mainly because:
options: Mouth pipetting risks ingestion of hazardous or toxic chemicals, making mechanical/manual fillers a much safer practice
Pipette fillers deliver a larger volume than mouth pipetting
Pipette fillers are required only for coloured solutions
Mouth pipetting is faster but less accurate
questions.correct_answer: Mouth pipetting risks ingestion of hazardous or toxic chemicals, making mechanical/manual fillers a much safer practice
questions.explanation: Mouth pipetting creates a serious risk of accidentally ingesting or inhaling corrosive, toxic, or infectious material, so pipette fillers or mechanical pumps are standard safe laboratory practice.

questions.question: In a practical exercise, a student determines the percentage of iron in an iron tablet by dissolving it in acid, reducing all iron to Fe2+, and titrating with standard KMnO4. If the reaction is 5Fe2+ + MnO4- + 8H+ to 5Fe3+ + Mn2+ + 4H2O, the mole ratio of Fe2+ to MnO4- used in the calculation is:
questions.explanation: The balanced equation shows 5 moles of Fe2+ react with every 1 mole of MnO4-, so this 5:1 ratio must be used to convert moles of permanganate used to moles of iron present.

questions.question: Why must glassware such as conical flasks and beakers used in a quantitative titration practical be clean but need not necessarily be completely dry, unlike a burette or pipette being filled with titrant?
options: Because any water remaining in the conical flask does not change the number of moles of analyte it contains, whereas water in a burette/pipette would dilute the measured volume of titrant/analyte itself
Because dirty glassware improves the accuracy of the titration
Because conical flasks are never rinsed with water at all
Because only the colour of the indicator matters, not the flask's contents
questions.correct_answer: Because any water remaining in the conical flask does not change the number of moles of analyte it contains, whereas water in a burette/pipette would dilute the measured volume of titrant/analyte itself
questions.explanation: Since a conical flask does not measure a precise volume, residual rinse water in it does not affect the total moles of analyte present; but a burette or pipette measures volume precisely, so any dilution there directly affects the calculated moles delivered.

questions.question: A student is asked to determine the concentration of copper(II) sulfate solution using a colorimeter. Which basic property of the copper(II) sulfate solution makes this colorimetric method possible?
options: Its distinct blue colour, arising from absorption of light in the visible region by the hydrated Cu2+ ion
Its ability to conduct electricity
Its boiling point
Its density relative to water
questions.correct_answer: Its distinct blue colour, arising from absorption of light in the visible region by the hydrated Cu2+ ion
questions.explanation: Colorimetric determination of copper(II) sulfate is possible because the hydrated Cu2+ ion has a characteristic blue colour due to absorption of light in the visible spectrum, whose intensity increases with concentration according to Beer's law.
